title: AI curriculum: Assistance must preserve intellectual development
desc: Documents educational activity while distinguishing task performance, durable learning, verification and context-specific professional judgment.

kps.k: The central issue is how to teach AI-enabled practice without allowing AI to replace the intellectual work that develops legal judgment.
kps.d: The ABA Task Force and Chicago’s strategy pair practical AI competence with independent reasoning, writing and ethical responsibility. This is not simply a choice between adoption and prohibition: schools can teach supervised AI use while requiring unaided work for particular learning objectives. The dispute concerns when students should use AI, which tasks they should perform independently and how instructors can establish that students—not just their submissions—have improved.

qs.q: They must not only instill traditional lawyering skills such as problem-solving and judgment, but they also need to acknowledge and support the reality that lawyers of the future will need to incorporate AI tools into legal service delivery.

kps.k: Curricular activity is well documented, but coverage statistics do not establish national adoption rates or adequate preparation.
kps.d: The ABA’s 2024 survey covered 29 responding schools: 55% reported dedicated AI classes and 83% reported curricular opportunities for effective use. Later reports repeat this evidence rather than independently corroborate it. Ambrogi’s August 2, 2026 analysis covered an archive snapshot of 128 schools; subsequent archive tabulations covered 163. These are changing inventories with different coverage and categories, not a longitudinal adoption measure. The archive also discloses extensive AI assistance and incomplete independent human confirmation. Institutional examples establish offerings, not learning gains, and Linna cautions that provision often remains basic.

qs.q: The results showed that 55% of the 29 respondent law schools offered classes on AI, and 83% reported availability of opportunities like clinics where students can learn how to use AI tools hands-on.

kps.k: Berkeley exposes a substantive disagreement over the breadth of restrictions, not over whether independent reasoning matters.
kps.d: Berkeley’s Summer 2026 policy protects cognitive development by restricting AI throughout credited writing, including brainstorming, editing and translation, as well as examinations. Related accounts document written instructor exceptions and dedicated AI courses, so it is not an unconditional institutional ban. Its critic accepts unaided foundational training but questions extending restrictions beyond first-year students, arguing that supervised practice teaches students to detect fabricated citations and faulty analysis before clients bear the risks. That client-risk argument is a prediction, not demonstrated harm. Ambrogi later qualifies his criticism: instructor opt-in is common in the catalogued policies, although he still regards Berkeley’s breadth as distinctive.

qs.q: It provides students with the opportunity to develop the skills they need to conceptualize, outline, draft, revise, and edit their work by forbidding the use of AI for these purposes in connection with work submitted for credit.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence Policy, UC Berkeley School of Law (effective Summer 2026) · Academia · 2026

qs.q: “Instructors have the discretion to deviate from this default rule, provided that they do so in writing and with appropriate notice and require students to disclose any authorized AI use,” it states.

kps.k: Emerging experimental evidence separates better AI-assisted work from durable learning and challenges categorical claims about cognitive harm or benefit.
kps.d: The Suffolk memorandum cites a randomized study of 137 upper-level law students in which newer tools improved work-product quality on at least four of six tasks. A separate 2026 randomized study of 91 Minnesota students found faster, stronger initial work without reduced subsequent unaided performance. During AI-assisted revision, weaker initial drafts improved while stronger drafts regressed. These task-specific findings do not establish long-term educational effects or settle policy for first-year novices. They support the memorandum’s recommendation to reassess current systems and examine the task, user, timing and manner of use rather than assume either inevitable skill erosion or reliable skill development.

qs.q: If your experience with generative AI is limited to an early or free version of ChatGPT, it is worth revisiting one of today’s leading systems using its most capable available setting.
qs.a: Recommended Next Steps on Artificial Intelligence and Teaching (memorandum to Suffolk Law faculty) · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Proposed AI literacy extends beyond prompting to verification, professional responsibility and context-specific judgment.
kps.d: WashU retains research fundamentals while teaching students to check AI results against conventional research; Boston College assesses verification, critique and revision. These approaches keep students responsible for the work they submit. The archive separately identifies instruction about AI’s legal consequences and instruction in using AI for legal work: governance electives do not necessarily supply practical proficiency. Closing the AI Readiness Gap proposes a universal foundation in technical literacy, professional responsibility and practical proficiency through required courses, with optional advanced study. Bliss’s proposal for mandatory credits remains conditional on AI becoming an important legal competency, while Chicago preserves choice among advanced electives.

qs.q: Students receive hands-on training in legal-specific generative AI platforms and develop the skills needed to evaluate AI-generated results, detect hallucinated or inaccurate content, and compare outcomes with traditional research methods.
qs.a: More Law Schools Embrace AI: Curriculum Integration Across Legal Education · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: The first—what students learn—is foundational gen AI literacy, organized around three pillars: technical literacy, professional responsibility, and practical proficiency.
qs.a: Closing the AI Readiness Gap: A Framework for Law Schools · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Assessment redesign seeks observable student reasoning, but controlled testing can sacrifice valuable sustained writing.
kps.d: Reported responses include secure in-class examinations, oral discussion of papers, presentations and staged permissions for AI use. Texas reports sharply reducing take-home examinations; Linda Anderson replaced a major writing assignment with a locked-down test, while using AI herself to help construct it. Chicago acknowledges the trade-off: supervised writing can establish original effort but loses extended independent work over days or weeks. Its strategy therefore develops a hybrid approach rather than claiming a completed solution. Permission to use AI for study, or access to an open-book exam, does not itself authorize AI-generated assessed work.

kps.k: Simulations and clinics offer a second educational role for AI: expanding practice opportunities and testing legal-service tools.
kps.d: Bliss and Closing the AI Readiness Gap propose AI tutors, debate partners and repeatable simulations with feedback. Reported implementations include interviewing, negotiation and oral-argument bots, while Suffolk and Vanderbilt projects develop tools for litigants and legal-aid organizations. These examples illustrate educational mechanisms and access-to-justice aims, not demonstrated comparative learning gains or reductions in unmet legal need. The ABA Year 2 Report adds an implementation qualification: legal-AI quality standards require developer adoption and continuing assessment, not merely their formulation.

kps.k: Practical implementation requires coordinated faculty support, explicit rules and continuous updating—not simply software access.
kps.d: The Suffolk memorandum supports faculty discretion only when instructors understand student use and communicate clear rules; otherwise, it considers stronger defaults warranted. The readiness framework assigns coordination across research, ethics, clinics, careers and technology support, supplemented by short programs as tools change. Upload restrictions separately address privacy, consent and course-material rights. Student Pulse commentary reports that 72% consider AI an essential professional skill, 74% fear over-reliance could impede legal-skill development and 32% reject the adequacy of their school’s preparation. These are perceptions, not competence measures. Predictions of employment advantages and rapid curricular obsolescence strengthen calls for adaptation but do not prove particular curricula effective.

qs.q: That approach preserves pedagogical discretion, but its effectiveness depends in part on the extent to which faculty know how students use the tools and whether faculty are communicating clear rules.

vlens.an: The curated academia-and-research sources collectively accept the proposition that legal education should develop AI competence without allowing assisted performance to substitute for the intellectual work that forms independent legal judgment. They materially extend it by supplying differentiated curricular models, assessment safeguards, verification and professional-responsibility requirements, institution-wide coordination frameworks, and emerging task-specific experimental evidence. Common reasons include preparing students for AI-enabled practice, preserving authorship and accountability, teaching critical evaluation of outputs, and matching AI permissions to learning objectives and student experience. Material variation concerns implementation rather than the core aim: Berkeley adopts broad default restrictions for credited work and examinations; Chicago combines protected foundational work with supervised use and optional advanced study; other authors favour universal baseline literacy, practical simulations, or conditionally mandatory credits. The Suffolk memorandum adds an empirical qualification: AI-assisted work can improve without necessarily weakening later unaided performance, but effects vary by task, user, timing and manner of use. Most sources describe policies, proposed mechanisms or educational aims rather than demonstrated durable learning gains, and the archive is explicitly an inventory rather than a prevalence survey.

qs.q: The feedback we have received throughout this process has been consistent: We need to ensure that our students actually learn to think critically, strategically, and independently without relying on AI; but we also must face the reality that AI tools are already widely available to our students, and our graduates will be expected to be prepared to use them in legal practice.
qs.a: Rethinking Legal Education in the AI Era (AI Strategy Statement) · Academia · 2026

vlens.an: This curated set of market-analysis, consultancy and press sources accepts the proposition’s core distinction between AI-assisted performance and the independent intellectual work needed to develop legal judgment. It materially extends that proposition by identifying concrete implementation models: supervised low-stakes practice in verification, curricula that combine research fundamentals with critique of AI output, instructor-authorised or staged use, experiential simulations, and secure or oral assessments that make student reasoning more observable. Common reasons are practice readiness, the need to detect hallucinated or otherwise faulty output, and concern that unrestricted AI use can obscure whether students themselves can reason and write. Material variation concerns the appropriate breadth of restrictions: one source criticises Berkeley’s rules beyond foundational first-year work, while another places Berkeley within a wider pattern of restricting AI in assessed work but teaching it elsewhere. Other reporting is more limited and descriptive, documenting uneven adoption, resource constraints and rapid curricular obsolescence without directly establishing durable learning gains. These sources should not be treated as representative of market analysts, consultancies or the press generally, and their institutional examples and policy inventories do not prove educational effectiveness.

qs.q: Students receive hands-on training in legal-specific generative AI platforms and develop the skills needed to evaluate AI-generated results, detect hallucinated or inaccurate content, and compare outcomes with traditional research methods.
qs.a: More Law Schools Embrace AI: Curriculum Integration Across Legal Education · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: Taken together, the data suggests law schools are converging on a common approach, which is to restrict AI in graded work and exams, but teach it everywhere else.

vlens.an: These selected regulators, courts and professional-body sources accept the proposition’s central balance: legal education should prepare students to use AI while preserving judgment, problem-solving, critical thinking and ethical responsibility. Their common rationale is that AI will be part of legal-service delivery, so prohibition or software access alone is inadequate; students need practical experience coupled with awareness of capabilities, limitations, risks and professional obligations. The Year 2 report materially develops the proposition by identifying concrete implementations—required certification, hands-on tool use, governance instruction, simulations and clinics—and by stressing continuous curricular updating, human-centred innovation and quality assessment. Internal variation is mainly one of scope and evidentiary strength: the Year 1 report states the broad educational and risk-management principle, whereas Year 2 supplies institutional examples and implementation priorities. Neither establishes durable learning gains, and the repeated 29-school survey describes respondents rather than national adoption. These curated sources should not be treated as representative of all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

qs.q: They must not only instill traditional lawyering skills such as problem-solving and judgment, but they also need to acknowledge and support the reality that lawyers of the future will need to incorporate AI tools into legal service delivery.

vlens.an: The legal-tech-vendor source supports the proposition that AI-enabled legal education must preserve students’ independent intellectual development and professional judgment. It treats AI competence and concern about over-reliance as complementary: the reported survey perceptions indicate that students see AI as professionally important while also fearing that excessive reliance could impede critical legal-skill development. It therefore advocates core AI instruction embedded in legal-practice contexts, with attention to risks, opportunities and personal accountability rather than tool use in isolation. Material variation lies in emphasis rather than direction: the source presses institutions to expand structured preparation but simultaneously rejects unqualified adoption and stresses that appropriate use differs by legal task. Its statistics measure student beliefs and perceived preparedness, not actual competence, learning gains or cognitive harm. Because the curated evidence contains one legal-tech-vendor source, this position should not be generalized to legal-tech vendors as a group.

elens.an: The 2023–2024 sources support the proposition that legal education should teach AI-enabled practice while preserving the intellectual work, judgment and responsibility required of lawyers. Their common rationale is that generative AI was becoming sufficiently capable and accessible that prohibition alone was impractical, but effective preparation required students to understand limitations, evaluate outputs, verify citations and facts, edit substantively and remain accountable for submitted work. Material variation concerns implementation rather than the proposition’s core: the ABA Task Force states a broad curricular balance between traditional lawyering skills and technology training; Generative Artificial Intelligence and the Practice of Law argues specifically for responsible use rather than bans, coupled with independent verification; and Bliss goes further by proposing concrete exercises involving evaluation, simulations and reflection, plus conditionally mandatory legal-AI credits. These sources mainly offer recommendations, reported curricular activity and anticipated professional needs—not empirical evidence of durable learning, preserved unaided reasoning or effective assessment design. Because the corpus is curated, their alignment should not be treated as evidence of prevalence across legal educators or institutions.

elens.an: The selected 2025 sources collectively accept the proposition that legal education should develop practical AI competence without displacing independent legal reasoning, and they materially extend it with concrete models: retaining research fundamentals, teaching verification and critique of AI output, combining hands-on tool use with ethics and regulation, and using simulations and clinics for supervised practice. Their common rationale is practice readiness under rapidly changing technology, coupled with continued human responsibility for assessing legal work. Material variation remains: the curriculum reporting addresses preservation of reasoning and verification directly; the infrastructure article more narrowly documents uneven adoption and likely curricular obsolescence without evaluating intellectual development; and the ABA Year 2 report broadens the approach to human-centred innovation, access-to-justice projects and developer quality standards. Across the sources, offerings and intended benefits are better documented than durable learning gains, and employment advantages, displacement and obsolescence are forecasts rather than demonstrated outcomes. Because these are curated and partly overlapping accounts, their number does not establish prevalence among law schools or educators.

qs.q: WashU Law is integrating AI as a tool to be used critically and effectively, not as a replacement for human legal reasoning.

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the proposition that legal education should prepare students for AI-enabled practice without allowing AI to replace the intellectual work through which legal judgment develops. They materially extend it by specifying differentiated curricular and governance mechanisms: protected unaided work for foundational or assessed tasks; supervised AI use for research, drafting, revision and simulations; explicit instruction in verification, professional responsibility and context-specific judgment; redesigned assessments that make student reasoning observable; and coordinated faculty support and course-level rules. The Suffolk memorandum adds limited experimental evidence that separates stronger AI-assisted work products from durable learning: effects varied by task, user, timing and manner of use, challenging categorical claims that AI either necessarily damages or reliably improves reasoning. Material variation concerns breadth, sequencing and institutional control rather than the core objective. Berkeley adopts unusually broad default restrictions across credited writing and exams, while its critic would concentrate restrictions in foundational training and expand low-stakes supervised practice. Chicago pursues a layered model combining protected first-year learning, supervised use and hybrid writing assessment; other sources favour universal baseline literacy followed by optional advanced study, staged permissions, disclosure rules, simulations or secure assessment. The archive and commentary document these approaches but do not establish national prevalence or learning gains, and student-survey figures measure perceptions rather than competence. No supplied source rejects the principal proposition; disagreement is primarily over how to operationalise the balance.
